description: I’m Shoaib Siddique, a software engineer who loves turning raw data into tools people can actually use. For Space Apps 2026 I built FireBridge, which merges 25 years of NASA MODIS and VIIRS fire data into one comparable record, with a fire chance map and alerts preview. My interests: web apps, data pipelines and climate and wildfire data. I’d welcome teammates with remote sensing, GIS, data science or UX/design skills, or anyone keen to make wildfire alerts reach the people who need them.
summary:
NASA has watched fires from space since 2000, first with MODIS and since 2012 with VIIRS. VIIRS sees much finer detail, so it counts 4 to 9 times more hot spots for the same fires. If you glue the two records together, fire seems to explode in 2012 (in Alberta, ×4.9 overnight), and that jump isn't real. This is why 25 years of data can't be used as one series.

FireBridge fixes this. For any area and each calendar month, it learns how MODIS counts compare with VIIRS counts in the years when both satellites were flying. It then converts the MODIS years into VIIRS terms, with an honest uncertainty band. The result is one continuous record from 2000 to today, in which Alberta's 2011 to 2012 change becomes +8% instead of ×4.9.

On top of that record, FireBridge shows when an area normally burns, whether this week is unusual, and which squares of the map are most likely to burn next week. Tested on 11 past years it never saw, it catches 51% of the squares that burned in Canada, against 10% for guessing. The goal is earlier, clearer warnings for agencies and the public.
details:
What it does. FireBridge turns two NASA fire records that don't match (MODIS from 2000, VIIRS from 2012) into one record you can trust, then uses it to answer three questions for any area: when does it usually burn, is this week unusual, and where is fire most likely next week.

How it works.

  1. Harmonisation. Hot spots from NASA FIRMS are filtered (low-confidence points removed, vegetation fires only) and counted per area, per month. For each calendar month, FireBridge learns the MODIS to VIIRS ratio from the overlap years (2012 onward), so a July is compared with other Julys. It converts the MODIS-only years into "VIIRS-equivalent" counts with a likely range. It also bridges the early Terra-only months (2000 to 2002) to Terra+Aqua, and scales NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 to Suomi NPP, which stopped delivering data on 2 Nov 2026. A "Retire MODIS" test hides recent VIIRS years and predicts them from MODIS alone. Its error is 13 to 27%, against 74 to 77% when the raw counts are used as they are.
  2. Burning calendar. A month-by-year heat map of the harmonised record shows each area's fire season, plus record years. For example, Alberta 2023 was 5 times the previous record.
  3. Fire chance map. For all of Canada, a model looks at 0.25° squares week by week. It uses the time of year, last year, burns in the past 3 years, the last 2 weeks of activity and station weather from NOAA, and ranks the squares most likely to burn next week. It is always trained only on years before the one it predicts. Tested on 2015 to 2025, its top 10% of squares catch 51% of burning squares (Manitoba 61%, Quebec 57%), against about 10% for random guessing.
  4. Alerts preview. A replay of a daily alert service: an alert fires when the last 7 days reach a chosen multiple of the usual for that time of year. For example, it would have sent an alert for Alberta on 30 Apr 2023, at 5.5 times normal, before the worst weeks. The preview shows the email, the text message and the agency (JSON) versions. Nothing is actually sent.

Benefits and impact. Researchers and agencies get a 25-year fire record they can compare across sensors, so trends and anomalies are real and not artefacts of a satellite change. Fire services get a weekly, map-based view of where risk is highest. The public could subscribe to plain-language alerts for the places they care about.

Tools. JavaScript, HTML and CSS (one self-contained web page, which runs entirely in the browser), Leaflet for the map, hand-built SVG charts, a logistic regression model written in JavaScript, and Python for the data pipeline (FIRMS downloads, gridding, NOAA GSOD weather processing). Basemaps come from Esri World Imagery and NASA GIBS.

What makes it creative. FireBridge doesn't stop at a correction factor. It shows the correction (glued vs harmonised record, with uncertainty), proves it on data it never saw, and turns the result into tools a person can act on: a calendar, a weekly chance map and alerts. Every section has an ⓘ panel that explains in plain words what you are looking at and what its limits are.

Factors we considered. We considered differences between sensors (pixel size, overpass time, the change of satellites in 2026), seasonal differences in the ratio, honest uncertainty instead of single numbers, no data leaking from the future into tests, plain language for non-specialists, and speed (the whole app works offline in one file).

Use of AI. The code, data pipeline and explanatory text were written with the help of an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic), directed and reviewed by the team. This is stated in the app's footer and page metadata. All numbers come from NASA and NOAA data.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System)
NASA FIRMS API: MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m active fire data (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21)
projectRefs: NOAA Global Surface Summary of the Day (GSOD) weather stations, AWS Open Data
Claude by Anthropic (AI assistant used for code and text)
